url.label: Called
url.address_help: The address somebody would actually type.
url.label_placeholder: left blank, the host is used
url.follow_redirects_help: Each redirect is checked as a new destination. A redirect into an unapproved private host is refused rather than followed.
url.ask_if_changed_help: Sends the last ETag, so an unchanged page answers 304 with no body. A 304 counts as healthy and skips the content check, because there is no body to check.
url.expected_status_help: 0 accepts anything from 200 to 399. A URL that should redirect, or an endpoint that correctly answers 401, is working — insisting on 200 would report it broken for ever.
url.keep_group_help: Which bracketed part of the pattern to record. Nearly always 1 — a pattern needs context around the part that matters. 0 keeps the whole match.
url.value_note: Taken from the response by the {{rule}} rule. This is the check that catches a page returning 200 with the wrong content, which nothing else here can see.
url.collector_interval_limit: The account’s cron runs about every {{interval}}, so a check set to run more often than that will run at that rate instead.
account.this_account: This account — the one this dashboard runs as.
account.root_unmanaged: root. This dashboard cannot stop or change these.
descriptions.sign_in_to_write: Sign in to write your own.
descriptions.empty: Nothing written yet. The built-in list covers {{processes, number}} processes and {{slabs, number}} slab caches; anything on this machine it does not know about shows its name with no mark beside it, which is how to find the ones worth writing down.
descriptions.forget_help: The note goes; the built-in description takes over again if there is one for that name, and otherwise the name appears with nothing beside it.
descriptions.bubble_own: Your own note. Click for the link and to edit it.
descriptions.bubble_link: Click to open this, with a link to more.
descriptions.owned_here: Written on this machine, about this machine.
descriptions.built_in_help: From the built-in list, which is guessing from the name. If you know better for this machine, write your own — it will replace this everywhere.
descriptions.slab_help: A kernel slab cache — memory the kernel itself is holding.
descriptions.process_help: A process running on this machine.
descriptions.saved: Saved. It shows beside that name from now on.
url.saved_answered: Saved, and it answered {{status}} in {{ms}} ms.
url.saved_failed: Saved, but the first check failed: {{detail}}.
url.notify_change_help: Raises an alert the moment the captured text is different from last time. This is how you watch a version string: what matters is not its value but when it moved. The alert obeys the usual cooldown, so a value that flaps does not flood — but every change is marked on the chart and listed under it either way.
regex.group_absence_help: A group that did not take part is not the same as one that matched nothing — an optional group is simply absent, and the check would record nothing on that run.
pending.schedule_unknown: The collector's schedule is not known yet, so there is no countdown to give.
pending.collector_overdue: The collector last ran {{age}} ago and runs every {{interval}} — this will not arrive until it runs again.
pending.past_due: {{duration}} past due — the collector may not be running
alerts.sent_legacy_title: Sent {{when}}. This one went out before messages were kept, so there is nothing to open.
alerts.muted_title: Delivery was held by a temporary operator mute. Click for details.
alerts.held_by_operator_mute: Held by a temporary operator mute
alerts.mute_detail_help: The event and its evidence were recorded normally. Error and Critical alerts bypass temporary mutes.
alerts.mail_not_delivered_help: This message was written and not delivered. It is kept anyway: “the email failed” is a fact about the mail system, and the thing worth having next is what it would have said.
alerts.mail_dialog_help: Kept as it was sent. The wording depends on what else fired in the same minute and on the settings at the time, so it cannot be worked out again afterwards — which is why it is stored rather than rebuilt.
alert.verdict_timing: The rule called this {{severity}} and raised it {{raised}}. {{assistant}}
alert.finding_recheck_queued: The finding will be checked again.
incident.captured_at: Captured {{time}} — the machine as it stood at that moment.
incident.unreadable: This record could not be read back.
incident.memory_by_service: Memory by service (PSS, from the host collector)
incident.by_category_since_scan: By category, since the previous scan
incident.files_grew_most_since_scan: Files that grew most, since the previous scan
alert.verdict_dialog_help: This is a language model’s opinion of a machine-generated alert. The alert itself is still here, still unread, and can be marked read or deleted like any other — nothing was thrown away.
process.trend_summary: Top {{count}} recorded process groups for the selected range. Recent reporters lead; peak {{metric}} users fill the remaining slots, so a resolved problem remains visible. Names join replacement PIDs into one line.
process.trend_empty_help: No busy process snapshots fall inside this range. Process history is recorded only when the configured CPU or memory threshold is crossed.
process.trend_empty: No recorded process load in this range
process.stop_unavailable: This one cannot be stopped from here.
process.stop_force_one_help: SIGKILL — it is killed outright, with no chance to finish writing anything
process.stop_force_many_help: SIGKILL — all {{count}} are killed outright, with no chance to finish writing anything
process.stop_ask_one_help: SIGTERM — it is asked to exit and can tidy up first
process.stop_ask_many_help: SIGTERM — each is asked to exit and can tidy up first
process.stop_force_waiting: {{name}} is still in the process list after SIGKILL. That normally means it is stuck in the kernel — waiting on a disk or a network mount — where no signal can reach it until whatever it is waiting for returns.
process.stop_ask_waiting: {{name}} was asked to stop and has not. It is entitled to ignore SIGTERM; Force sends a signal it cannot ignore.
process.stop_force_confirm:
Force {{what}} to stop?

SIGKILL cannot be caught or ignored. Anything part-way through being written stays part-way written.
process.stop_ask_confirm:
Ask {{what}} to stop?

SIGTERM lets it close its files and exit cleanly. It can also ignore this.
process.rank_second_largest: The second largest in this column.
process.cpu_help: ps measures each process against one core, so anything threaded can pass 100%. The CPU figure on the overview is a share of the whole machine and is a different measurement.
process.unavailable: Cannot read the process list here.
process.no_matches: Nothing among the {{scanned}} running processes matches that.
process.matches_all_protected: Matches {{matched}} of the {{scanned}} running processes; all are protected.
process.matches_some_protected: Matches {{matched}} of the {{scanned}} running processes; {{blocked}} are protected.
process.all_matches_protected: Every match is protected, so there is nothing here to stop.

editor.review_no_changes: No changes since this file was opened.
editor.review_help: Removed lines start with − and added lines start with +. This is a review only; saving still uses the protected atomic write.
editor.view_help: This file is shown for review only. Find works locally; no text is sent back to the server.
editor.browser_more: {{count}} additional entries not shown. Open a narrower directory to keep browsing responsive.
editor.browser_help: Only direct children are shown. Symbolic links are never followed here, and opening a file repeats its path and access checks.

display.speaking_help: Browser speech synthesis; replies are read aloud only when enabled.
display.voice_help: Available voices come from this browser and device.
display.listening_help: After applying, click Start listening to grant microphone permission. Push to talk requires holding the Listen button; Always on restarts recognition until stopped.
peers.admin_only: Only administrators can manage trusted servers.

encryption.bootstrap_recovery_notice: Bootstrap configuration recovery is deliberately CLI-only: `scripts/restore-config.php` authenticates and parses the sealed PHP without executing it, atomically replaces `lib/config.php`, and leaves the prior configuration as a sealed rollback artifact. Test the recovered settings before deleting that artifact.
encryption.superseded_copies_notice: Superseded copies remain encrypted with an earlier local key after rotation. Keep that key until you have completed a replacement-key recovery drill; they are not deleted automatically.
scan.host_collector_disabled: The host collector is not enabled, so none of these run.
scan.dashboard_browsing: Somebody has the dashboard open right now (last seen {{when}}), so anything set to speed up while browsing is currently on its shorter interval.
ai.interrupted_with_runs: Stopped. {{runs}} it had started was dropped.
ai.interrupted: Stopped. Tell it what you want it to do instead.
scan.started: Scan started. It runs in the background — the tables update when it finishes.
alerts.delete_confirm: Delete this alert? The history goes with it.
auth.end_sessions_confirm: End every signed-in session? This immediately signs out every browser, including this one. Use it if a device is lost or access may be compromised.
auth.recovery_codes_create_help: This replaces every previous recovery code. Store the new one-time codes offline; Zogograph will show them only once.
auth.recovery_codes_save_help: Each code works once in place of the authenticator code. This is the only time Zogograph can display them; store them offline and do not put them in a password manager shared with your sign-in password.
problems.clear_confirm:
Clear the problem log?

The entries are removed for good. Anything still broken will write a fresh one on its next failure, which is the point: what is left afterwards is what is still wrong.
audit.clear_confirm:
Clear every earlier audit entry?

This action stays as the first new audit entry.
audit.export_confirm:
Download the full audit history as CSV?

It can contain private paths and client addresses. Store the file securely.

auth.recovery_codes_ready: Eight new one-time recovery codes are ready to save.

terminal.recovery_restored: Restored {{path}}; the prior version was copied for recovery.
terminal.recovery_help: Private pre-save copy. Restoring creates a new copy of the current version.
terminal.syntax_preview_help: This local, read-only preview never executes or sends file contents. The native editor remains the place to edit and save.
terminal.copy_refused: This browser would not let the page write to the clipboard.
terminal.copy_manually: Select the command and copy it — this browser would not.
terminal.bell_title: The command rang the terminal bell
terminal.limits: Runs as this account with {{shell}}. Anything still going after {{duration}} is stopped, and output stops at {{output}}.
terminal.switch_off_consequence: This withdraws the permission, not just the unlock. Anything running now is stopped and the page goes back to offering a switch.
terminal.switch_off_retention: Nothing is lost - the transcript of what has been run stays in the action log, and you can switch it on again whenever you want it.
terminal.sign_in_to_enable: Sign in to switch it on.
terminal.enabled_locked: The terminal is switched on. It is still locked until you open it.
terminal.config_disabled: lib/config.php has it off, which is the default. Switching it on here overrules that and is remembered; the config file is not rewritten.
terminal.locked_help: The terminal is locked. It locks itself after a while on purpose — an always-open shell is one that whoever gets this password inherits. Open it for as long as you need and it will close on its own.
terminal.enable_title: Allow a shell in this web page?
terminal.enable_warning_execution: This runs whatever is typed into it, as the user the web server runs as, and shows the output. It is a web shell.
terminal.enable_warning_password: That means anybody who has this dashboard's password has it too. If that password is shared, or is the only thing between the internet and this machine, decide about that first.
terminal.enable_warning_audit: Every command is written to the action log before it runs, so a command that hangs the machine still appears in the record. It stays locked until you open it, and it locks itself again after the time you choose.
terminal.enable_warning_disable: You can switch it off again here at any time.
setup.form_held: Not refreshed while you are editing. Save, or move away and come back, to see what is stored.
package.lift_confirmation:
Lift the revocation for {{id}}?

The package remains disabled. Review its files and explicitly grant/enable it again only if you trust it.
package.revoke_reason_help: Revocation disables this package immediately and records why. Lifting it later still leaves the package disabled until capabilities are explicitly granted again.
package.remove_confirmation:
Remove {{id}} {{version}}?

This removes its immutable package files and registry record. Package-private data and encrypted secrets are retained so they can be recovered or reused after a future reinstall.
package.review_altered: Review or remove altered files before enabling.
package.grant_all_enable: Grant every listed capability and enable
package.sign_in_review: Sign in to review executable packages.
package.runtime_intro: A package must have a trusted publisher, a valid signed file manifest, and every requested capability granted explicitly. The dashboard never loads package PHP. A separate worker can only perform a no-secret capability probe inside an operator-attested OS/container sandbox; it does not enable provider operations.
package.no_trusted_publishers: No executable-package publisher keys are trusted yet. Add a publisher key in setup before installing a signed package.
package.none_installed: No signed executable packages are installed.
package.archive_help: The archive is extracted privately, then every file hash and the publisher signature are verified before installation. It stays disabled until you explicitly grant capabilities and enable it.
auth.password_required_current: Choose a password. The current one cannot be carried over into text shown to somebody who has not entered it.
setup.error_detail: Setup could not complete this action: {{detail}}
setup.help.openid_enabled: Lets explicitly registered trusted applications sign users in through this Zogograph installation. It does not make this server a public identity service.
setup.help.openid_issuer: The HTTPS URL trusted clients use to discover this provider, for example https://monitor.example.com. Do not include a trailing slash.
setup.help.openid_signing_private_key: Required before enabling the provider. Use a dedicated RSA private key; never reuse the TLS certificate key. Setup can generate a dedicated key that is kept only in the protected setup session until this section is saved.
setup.help.scan_root: Everything is measured under here, and nothing outside it can ever be deleted.
setup.help.timezone: Used for the timestamps on the dashboard and in alert emails.
setup.help.encryption_mode: Off keeps all current storage unencrypted. Sealed copies make separately encrypted, verified snapshots; they do not alter the live database or its journal. Host-managed volume protection is configured and operated outside Zogograph.
setup.help.package_runtime_trusted_keys: Optional. Add only a publisher key you independently trust. Each key id maps to a publisher name and Base64 Ed25519 public_key. A signed package cannot install unless its publisher and key match this list.
setup.help.package_runtime_secret_key_fi: An absolute private key file outside this web directory. Leave blank to reuse the local encryption key when configured. Without either key, package secret references cannot be saved. A separate file gives package credentials separate custody.
setup.help.encryption_key_custody: The built-in sealed-copy mode currently uses one private local key file. Fleet, manual-unlock, and marketplace key providers will be selectable only when their secure protocols are installed and tested.
setup.help.encryption_key_file: Create it first with scripts/encryption-key.php. It must be an absolute, non-symlink file outside this web directory and readable only by the Zogograph service account.
setup.help.encryption_artifact_directory: Leave blank for data/sealed. Use an absolute private path to keep encrypted copies elsewhere.
setup.help.encryption_stores: The recommended start protects bootstrap configuration, setup, and account data. Add host or assistant stores when you want their process evidence or conversations protected too; those optional stores wait until they exist.
setup.help.encryption_backup_schedule: Zogograph records this preference; configure the matching cron or host-scheduler job. Manual creates copies only when cron.php --seal is run.
setup.help.encryption_retention_days: Zero means keep every copy. During an explicit sealing run, Zogograph prunes only old verified local artifacts whose ciphertext hash still matches, and never the newest verified copy for a store.
setup.help.encryption_retention_days_by_: Optional JSON object, for example {"setup":365,"account":30}. Zero keeps every copy for that store. Stores not listed use the normal retention target.
setup.help.encryption_recovery_drill_max: Zogograph warns when a selected store has not completed a non-destructive recovery drill within this period. Ninety days is the recommended starting point; zero disables periodic reminders after the first required drill.
setup.help.encryption_retention_recovery: Optional JSON object such as {"daily":7,"weekly":4,"monthly":12}. It preserves the newest verified copy from each distinct UTC day, week, or month in addition to normal retention. Zero or omitted tiers keep the simple retention target.
setup.help.password: Reveals real paths and enables deleting. Leave blank to disable sign-in, which leaves the dashboard readable with every path masked.
setup.help.alerts_enabled: The point of the thing: it tells you before the disk fills, not after.
setup.help.alerts_from: Blank uses whatever the server sends as by default.
setup.help.disk_free_bytes: Write it how you say it: 5G, 500M, or a plain number of bytes.
setup.help.projected_full_hours: Fitted over the last day of readings. This is the alert that arrives while there is still time to do something.
setup.help.path_jump_bytes: The alert that names the culprit rather than the symptom.
setup.help.cpu_percent: Sustained, not a spike: it has to hold across the whole window below. Zero turns it off. On CloudLinux this is a share of what the account may use, not of the machine.
setup.help.cpu_minutes: A burst cannot hold across a long window, which is the whole point of measuring duration rather than height.
setup.help.cooldown_seconds: Written how you say it: 6h, 90m, 2d. A plain number is seconds. An alert that arrives every minute becomes a filter rule within a day.
setup.help.anomalies_enabled: Compares each service, category and file against its own history. It catches the things no threshold can - a job that normally takes two minutes still running after an hour - and stays quiet about the nightly backup that always grows. Says nothing until it has history to say it from.
setup.help.anomalies_min_readings: Below this it says nothing at all. Too low and its first day is all false alarms, which is how these get turned off.
setup.help.anomalies_service_percent: Against its own median over the last day, not against a fixed size. A service that grows and stays grown is leaking; one that grows and comes back was busy.
setup.help.deletable_categories: Only ever by a signed-in session, and only inside the watched directory.
setup.help.host_enabled: Adds a second collector, run by root from WHM, that sees what this account cannot: other users' processes and memory, kernel slab caches, and root-owned logs under /etc. On CloudLinux this is the only way to find out what is using the machine.
setup.help.core_features_assistant: Disabling this removes the assistant from the dashboard and blocks its API routes. Existing assistant settings and private data are retained for a later re-enable.
setup.help.core_features_overview: Disabling this removes the Overview dashboard and its shared measurements. The shell keeps only the feature and access state needed to open another enabled page; collection continues unchanged.
setup.help.core_features_peers: Disabling this removes trusted servers from the dashboard and refuses its API, telemetry, and connection routes. Existing peer settings and private data are retained for a later re-enable.
setup.help.core_features_marketplace: Disabling this removes Marketplace from the dashboard and blocks its API routes. Installed marketplace metadata and revision history are retained for a later re-enable.
setup.help.core_features_terminal: Disabling this removes the Terminal and its sessions from the dashboard, blocks its API routes, and prevents assistant tools from reading terminal history. Existing private terminal evidence is retained for a later re-enable.
setup.help.core_features_notes: Disabling this removes notes, database copies, chart annotations, and broadcasts from the dashboard and blocks their API routes. Existing notes and captured evidence are retained for a later re-enable.
setup.help.core_features_problems: Disabling this removes Recent problems, its dashboard badges, and its API routes. Zogograph continues recording server errors so diagnostics and support remain safe.
setup.help.core_features_storage: Disabling this removes account storage, its file views, data controls, and retention controls from the dashboard; blocks their read, management, and assistant APIs; and preserves scans, configured retention, and safe server-side rollups.
setup.help.core_features_audit: Disabling this removes the Audit page and blocks its API routes and assistant history tool. Zogograph continues recording accountability entries server-side.
setup.help.core_features_metadata: Disabling this removes Custom names and What things are from the dashboard and blocks their API routes. Existing labels and descriptions are retained for a later re-enable.
setup.help.core_features_notifications: Disabling this removes Email alerts from the dashboard and blocks its configuration and test API routes. Existing alert delivery settings and server-side alert evaluation continue unchanged.
setup.help.core_features_backups: Disabling this removes the Backup inspection pages and blocks their API route. It does not alter backups or their provider-managed schedules.
setup.help.core_features_encryption: Disabling this removes Protection and blocks its on-demand status and recovery APIs. Configured encrypted-copy schedules and server-side verification continue unchanged.
setup.help.core_features_alerts: Disabling this removes Alerts, its shared dashboard badge and banner, and its API routes. Server-side alert evaluation and configured delivery continue unchanged.
setup.help.core_features_uptime: Disabling this removes Uptime and blocks its API route. It does not alter host or account collector schedules.
setup.help.core_features_packages: Disabling this removes Package runtime and package-contributed pages from the dashboard, blocks package-management APIs, and stops loading package language catalogs. Installed package records and their private settings remain intact for a later re-enable.
setup.help.core_features_charts: Disabling this removes Over time, blocks chart catalog and series APIs, and prevents assistant chart tools from reading or rendering chart history. Collectors and the current overview remain available.
setup.help.core_features_health: Disabling this removes the System health and self-diagnostic dashboard, blocks its presentation and diagnosis APIs, and hides overview findings. Setup checks and server-side collector safety checks continue to run.
setup.help.core_features_network: Disabling this removes network views and blocks their API, outbound lookup, capture, URL/domain, reverse-DNS, and calendar actions. Existing outbound safety, allow-list, and rate-limit controls remain enforced whenever it is enabled.
setup.help.core_features_host: Disabling this removes host, CPU, process, filesystem, capability, and change views; blocks their APIs, assistant tools, and on-demand host-task requests. Root-owned collection and its configured schedule continue unchanged.
setup.help.host_owner: Root creates the host database, so without this only root can read it and the panel stays empty. Almost always the cPanel username.
setup.help.host_watch: Apache writes each domain's logs under /etc owned by root, where a rotated log can reach several hundred megabytes invisibly. Shell globs.
setup.help.host_keep_days: A host reading is much bigger than an account one - it carries every user, the biggest processes and the slab table.

setup.basics_help: Review these checks, then open Security to create the sign-in password. All other settings are available from the navigation when you need them.
setup.basics_first_run_help: Create the sign-in password to finish the first step. Installation checks stay below it; other settings appear after the password is saved.
setup.not_configured_help: Until you finish, anybody who can reach this page can set the password. Do it now; afterwards this remains the password-protected configuration backend.
setup.no_password_help: There is no secret to prove, so nothing can authorize replacing the configuration from here. Fill this in and paste the result into lib/config.php yourself — having a file to edit is the authorization.
setup.configured_help: Enter the current password below and this will replace lib/config.php. Without it you still get the finished text to copy and paste.
setup.saved_section: This section is now stored in data/setup.db.
setup.first_readings: Take the first readings, then open the dashboard:
setup.keep_setup: Keep setup.php available for later administrator changes. It requires the current password before it can replace your configuration.
setup.root_install_help: The host collector cannot be installed from here — it runs as root, and this page runs as your account. Log in to WHM or SSH as root and add this to root’s crontab (crontab -e):
setup.root_verify_help: Then run it once by hand to see that it works — without the schedule, and without --quiet so it tells you what it found:
setup.root_schedule_help: Until it runs, the whole-machine panel on the dashboard will say so rather than showing anything. The dashboard’s schedule editor cannot manage this job: it edits your account’s crontab, and this one belongs to root.
setup.copy_config_help: Replacing the whole file. Keep it out of reach — lib/.htaccess already denies the directory.
setup.new_mask_warning: This text carries a new mask secret, so using it renames every masked path on the dashboard.
encryption.package_key_intro: Create a separate key for optional separate custody of package credentials. It is stored with owner-only permissions in the same hidden private directory as the primary encryption key and protected by an Apache deny policy.
encryption.package_key_exists: Package-secrets key already exists at this location; this step is complete.
encryption.private_key_intro: Creates a Base64 256-bit key outside the web directory, with owner-only permissions and an Apache deny policy for its private directory.
encryption.key_path: New private key-file path (leave blank to use this location)
encryption.private_key_exists: Private key already exists at this location; this step is complete.
encryption.unlock_to_create: Unlock setup with the current password before creating this key.
privacy.masked_paths_help: Signed-out visitors see stable anonymous labels instead of real filesystem paths. Rotating this secret changes every one of those labels, breaking any old label-to-path correlation. Leave it unchanged unless you suspect it was exposed.
deployment.profile_intro: Save the target and update policy here. Credentials and SSH host keys are encrypted separately and the profile retains only opaque references. Plain FTP is not available; choose explicit TLS FTP where SSH is unavailable.
deployment.host_key_reference: SSH host-key reference (not used for FTPS)
deployment.store: Store deployment credential or host key
deployment.store_help: Paste one password, private key, or known_hosts entry. It is encrypted with the configured local key and shown only as an opaque reference after storage.
deployment.copy_release_help: Upload the ZIP made from the selected remote-core release. Copying always repeats the target and credential check first. The ZIP is unpacked only in a private temporary directory, and its contents are removed after transfer.
deployment.review_transport_help: This is a secret-free argument preview only. Braced values are supplied by the reviewed worker at test/copy time; saving or opening this preview makes no network connection.
deployment.handoff_help: Copy this nonsecret JSON into the remote Setup import form after unlocking it. It includes the controller address, update policy, and selected package groups; it never includes deployment credentials, host keys, pairing credentials, or local passwords.
deployment.save_to_review: Save a complete deployment profile to review its planned transport.
package.settings_help: These settings are validated against the signed package schema. Setup does not load package code to render this panel.
package.settings_json_help: Use only package-scoped secret_ref: values for credentials. Raw tokens and private keys are refused.
package.secret_references_help: Select a reference already stored for this package. The secret value is never shown or copied into this page. Create a new secret from the dashboard’s Packages area first if this list is empty.
package.secret_value_help: This value is encrypted in setup.db with your external package/encryption key. It is never returned after saving.
package.secret_reference_created_help: Copy this opaque reference into the package settings. It is the only value that settings will retain.
package.secret_empty: No encrypted package secrets have been stored. Add a secret to create an opaque reference; its value cannot be shown later.
package.secret_all_in_use: Every stored reference is in use. Save a replacement reference in package settings before deleting an older credential.
package.secret_unused_reference_help: Only unused references can be deleted. The secret value is never displayed.
package.secret_delete_confirmation: Delete this unused encrypted secret? Its value cannot be recovered from {{brand}} after deletion.
package.fix_settings_json: Fix the package settings JSON before choosing a secret reference.
schedule.intro: Choose the account collector cadence and apply it here. Only Zogograph’s marked cron block is changed; every other account cron job stays untouched.
schedule.collector_help: Vitals are lightweight readings. A scan walks the monitored directory and is normally left off or scheduled much less often.
schedule.offset_help: Offsets apply to a profile; Custom cron uses the five fields below directly.
schedule.custom_help: Used only when Custom five-field cron is selected. Standard cron has minutes, hours, day of month, month, and day of week; seconds are intentionally not supported.
support.provider_message_help: Explains what was measured and requests only safe actions. It deliberately does not ask anyone to delete anything in the backup directory.

dns.no_domains_watched: No domains are being watched yet. Add one on Domain names, then come back — a zone sweep is offered for domains you have said you care about rather than for any name, because it is a few dozen lookups against somebody's nameserver.
dns.dig_unavailable: dig is not available to this account, so zones cannot be looked up here. On Red Hat it is in bind-utils; on Debian, dnsutils.
dns.no_records_sweep: Nothing recorded for this domain yet. Press “Look it all up”.
dns.inventory_summary_last: {{records, number}} records across {{names, number}} names, last looked up {{last}}.
dns.group.delegation: Who is in charge of the zone

network.private_address_help: A private address — you are on the same network as this machine, or behind a proxy that is.
network.unlabelled_address_help: This address has no name yet. Naming it means it is recognised wherever it appears — in captures, in the connection list, in the ports table.
network.owner_mismatch_help: These differ. Every “permission denied” on this install traces back to that: the process cannot write what the other account owns.
network.proxy_claims_help: These are set by whatever spoke to the web server last. Behind a proxy they carry the real address; sent straight to the server they can say anything at all. The address above is the only one this process observed.

domain.no_lock_status: No registry lock status was returned.

whois.asking_registry: Asking the registry… this can take a few seconds.
whois.host_pending: WHOIS is not available to this account, so root's collector has been asked to run it. It answers on its next run — the countdown is at the top of the page, and this page will have the answer once it lands.
whois.host_pending_with_error: WHOIS is not available to this account, so root's collector has been asked to run it. It answers on its next run — the countdown is at the top of the page, and this page will have the answer once it lands. The last attempt on the host said: {{error}}
whois.host_answered: Answered by root's collector {{when}}, because WHOIS is not available to this account.
whois.available_name: {{name}} appears to be unregistered. The registry has no record of it, which is what an available name looks like — though a registry that is simply not answering can look the same, so check with a registrar before celebrating.
whois.no_recognized_date: The answer contained no date this dashboard recognizes

dns.sign_in_lookup: Sign in to run name lookups.
dns.query_wait: Asking… a server that does not reply takes three seconds to give up on, so this can take a few.
dns.query_freshness: {{asked}}, run {{at}}. These do not refresh on their own — each one sends a real query, and a page that repeated them every few seconds would be adding to the traffic it is measuring.
dns.machine_nameserver: This machine is listening on port 53, so it is a nameserver. Its own traffic will dwarf everything else here — see What is on the wire.

regex.sample_placeholder: Paste some of the page here — view source and take the part you are matching against.
regex.dialog_help: Nothing here is saved or requested on a schedule. It runs the pattern exactly the way the check will, against whatever you paste.
regex.initial_help: Paste some text and press Test it. Every match is shown with its groups numbered, so you can see which number to keep.

rdns.queue_both_collectors: Both collectors take one, so it may be quicker than that.
rdns.released_requests: {{count, number}} requests had been taken by a collector that never came back — a run killed mid-lookup — and have been put back in the queue.

telegram.test_failed: Could not send the Telegram test.

installed.empty: Nothing recorded yet. This is gathered when capabilities are checked.
installed.fingerprint_note: A value beginning “file” is a fingerprint, not a version: that program offers no readable version, so a change can be detected but not described.
email.enabled_help: Nothing is sent while this is off, however bad things get.
email.send_to_help: Several addresses, separated by semicolons. Each gets its own message rather than one with everybody in the To — a single send fails as a unit, so one bad mailbox would mean nobody hears.
email.send_from_help: Optional. Some hosts reject mail with no From header; others rewrite it whatever you put here.
email.dashboard_address_help: So the messages can link to the page that answers the question. The cron that sends them has no request to work this out from, so it has to be written down — otherwise a message says what is wrong and leaves you to find the page at two in the morning.
email.what_to_send: What to send about, and when

alerts.active_mutes_detail: Muted Information and Warning events remain visible with their delivery reason. Error and Critical alerts always bypass a mute.
alerts.mute_explainer: Mute “{{rule}}”? Matching Information and Warning alerts stay recorded but are not sent. Error and Critical always bypass this mute.

alerts.ignored_help: The rule called this {{severity}}. {{assistant}} concluded it did not warrant sending.

merge.upload_intro: Upload an exported Zogograph account SQLite database to review it. The review reads only collector paths, vitals, scans, totals, and path sizes; it never copies accounts, passwords, alerts, settings, packages, or audit history. Nothing changes until you explicitly apply the reviewed merge.
merge.review_expiry: This review expires in {{minutes, number}} minutes. The live database is checked again when you apply it.
merge.overlap_yes: Yes — duplicates are skipped by timestamp
merge.apply_help: Stop the account collector cron jobs and any dashboard writers first. Applying creates a private rollback snapshot, upgrades a private clone of the import when needed, then merges collector rows in one transaction.
merge.writers_stopped: I stopped all dashboard and collector writers.
merge.allow_overlap: I understand overlapping vitals and scans are deduplicated by timestamp.
merge.last_result: Last collector merge: {{paths, number}} paths, {{vitals, number}} vitals, and {{scans, number}} scans added. A private rollback snapshot was retained.
auth.password_keep: Leave blank to keep the current password.
auth.app_intro: Use an authenticator app such as Google Authenticator, 1Password, or Authy for a six-digit second factor. The secret is not saved until the app proves it can create a correct code.
auth.recovery_help: They will not be shown again. Each code works once if your authenticator is unavailable.
auth.recovery_confirm: I saved these recovery codes somewhere safe.
auth.enter_secret: Enter this secret into your authenticator app:

openid.provider_intro: This installation can already act as an OpenID Connect provider for trusted applications. Enable it only after setting its public HTTPS issuer, a dedicated signing key, and registered client redirect URLs. The provider supports authorization code with PKCE, discovery, JWKS, and signed ID tokens.
openid.provider_clients: Client registrations are managed below as structured settings; each client needs an exact redirect URL and a private client secret.
openid.key_ready: A new key is ready in this protected setup session. Save this section to commit it; it is not included in notices or logs.
openid.key_generation: Generation creates a new 3072-bit RSA key in this protected setup session. It is not committed until you save this section.
openid.trusted_apps_intro: Each application gets one exact HTTPS callback URL and a generated confidential-client secret. Existing secrets are never shown again; remove and recreate a client to rotate one.
openid.secret_once: It will not be shown again after acknowledgement.
update.available: A newer Zogograph update is available. Reload when you are ready.
update.compatibility: A compatibility update is ready. Reload before continuing so this browser uses the matching dashboard.
encryption.custody_notice: Optional remote key custody adds a separately authorized recovery envelope; it is not live-database encryption and does not upload a database or ciphertext. Before using it, configure the signed custody package, verify its endpoint and enrolled credential, review its dedicated sandbox launcher, and keep local recovery enabled. Ciphertext replica storage remains a separate future capability. Never enter a custody or relay management token, billing credential, plaintext database, or recovery key into this client.
cpu.limit_faults: {{faults, number}} CPU fault(s) recorded at the last reading across {{accounts, number}} account(s). A fault is an account asking for more processor than its LVE allows and being held back — this is being throttled now, not being near a limit. A throttled account's own percentage sits calmly at its ceiling, which is why the fault count is the figure to watch and not the percentage.
cpu.spread_not_measured: No per-core percentages yet. Each one is a difference between two readings, so the first collection after this feature was added has nothing to compare against.
cpu.spread_one_core: One core, so there is no distribution to look at — the whole-machine figure is the core's figure.
cpu.spread_shape: Busiest core {{busiest, number}}%, quietest {{quietest, number}}%, {{average, number}}% on average across {{cores, number}} cores.
cpu.spread_all_pinned: {{shape}} Every core is pinned: the machine has no processor headroom at all. Unlike a single busy core this does respond to more cores — but it is worth checking first that the work is work you wanted done.
cpu.spread_single_threaded: {{shape}} That is the shape of a single-threaded bottleneck: one piece of work that cannot be split, holding things up while the machine looks mostly free. The whole-machine percentage will never look alarming however stuck it gets, and more cores would not move it.
cpu.spread_even: {{shape}} The work is spreading evenly, so the only question left is how much of it there is.
cpu.spread_uneven: {{shape}} Uneven, but not one core carrying everything — normal on a machine running a mixture of jobs, and worth a second look if the gap keeps widening.
cpu.no_breakdown: No processor breakdown in this range yet — the collector records it from the version that added these pages onward
cpu.only_one_reading: Only one reading so far — a percentage needs two
cpu.add_root_cron: As root — ssh in or use WHM's Terminal — add this to root's crontab with crontab -e:
cpu.run_root_once: Then run it once by hand to see what it finds: {{command}}

host.status.title: Host collector status
host.request_queued: Asked. It runs on the host collector's next pass.
host.status.intro: These checks use the host database as the dashboard account can read it. Root collection is required for host-wide results; an account-run collector records only its own visible subset. This page can inspect this account’s crontab, but cannot read root’s crontab.
host.status.run_root: Run this once as root after saving Host settings:
page.title: {{page}} — {{brand}} infrastructure observation
chart.nothing_collected_range: Nothing collected for this range yet
storage.host_logs_help: The logs named in host_log_paths belong to root and live outside this account. On most shared servers they will be listed and refused, which is itself the answer. Where the host grants read access, they open in the same viewer as the account's own logs.
storage.sort_hour: Grew most in the last hour
storage.masked_names: Names are hidden until you sign in. The sizes and the growth are real.
tree.sign_in: Sign in to explore the disk.
tree.directory_empty: Nothing to show in this directory
backup.share_unknown: Share of the disk unknown — no filesystem reading recorded.
backup.walk_incomplete: The disk walk ran out of time, so this total is a lower bound.
backup.directories_not_opened: {{count}} directories under the backup roots were never opened.
backup.unattributed_help: Some of this could not be tied to an account. Nothing under the backup root carried a name matching a directory in /home, and JetBackup's own records were not readable — so it is reported as unattributed rather than assigned to the only account on the machine, which would be a guess.
backup.inferred_accounts_help: Accounts inferred from directory names under the backup root — JetBackup's own metadata was not readable, so these are a reasonable guess rather than its records.
backup.unmeasured_entries_help: {{count}} entries here could not be measured before the walk ran out of time. They are listed with no size rather than omitted. Raise host.walk_seconds and run it again for a complete figure.
backup.other_help: Directories that look like backups but are not managed by anything: a tar.gz somebody made before an upgrade, a dated copy of a site, a database dump. Nothing rotates these, so they stay for ever and are usually the oldest large thing on the disk. Probable is the operative word — each is a guess from the name and shape, and worth looking at before acting.
backup.safe_actions: Safe — returns space the backup system already considers disposable
backup.review_actions: Worth reviewing — a decision, not a chore
backup.dangerous_actions: Dangerous — listed so it can be named, not recommended
terminal.unavailable_reason: {{reason}} There is nothing this page can do about that, and nothing it should try — a host that has taken shell functions away has taken them away on purpose.
terminal.switched_off_help: The terminal is switched off. It is off by default because it runs whatever is typed into it — that is not a reason to avoid it, but it is a reason for the decision to be deliberate rather than inherited from a sample file.
backup.no_suggestions: Nothing to suggest from this reading.
backup.jetbackup_help: What the backup system says about its own backups is the only place the account and date behind a directory called files0000000005 can be found. It needs the JetBackup command line tool and usually needs running as root.
network.ports_public_empty: Nothing is listening on an address reachable from outside.
network.public_risky_port_tip: This normally has no authentication by default. Reachable from off the machine, that is a serious exposure rather than a configuration choice.
network.peers_empty: No established connections were recorded. Either the machine is idle, or ss could not be run by the collector.
network.private_address: a private address — another machine on this network
network.captures_empty: No captures have been taken yet. Ask for one on What is on the wire.
network.own_label_tip: A name you gave this, under Settings → Your own names.
network.rdns_name_tip: What the internet says this address is called — a PTR record, which its owner controls and can set to anything.
network.rdns_waiting_tip: Waiting to be looked up. One is resolved per collector run.
network.rdns_none_tip: Looked up: this address has no PTR record, so it has no name to show. That is a real answer, not a failure.
network.rdns_ask_tip: Queue a reverse lookup for this address
network.rdns_queued_tip: Queued. One is resolved per collector run.
network.rdns_taken_tip: A collector has already taken this one
network.rdns_no_name_tip: The address resolved, and the answer is that it has no PTR record. That is a real answer and is remembered, so it is not asked again for a week.
network.rdns_stale_tip: Older than {{age}}. Ask again to refresh it.
network.rdns_ask_again_tip: Queue another lookup — names do change
alert.rule_advice: What would let the rule decide this itself
uptime.track_unreadable: its database cannot be read from this account, so nothing can be said about whether it is running
uptime.track_last_late: last one {{duration}} ago — later than usual
chart.compaction_bucket: Each point covers {{duration}} and shows the worst value in that period, not an average.
chart.compaction_disk: The oldest readings here are also compacted on disk, up to {{readings, number}} readings to a row. Readings from around an alert are never compacted.
host.swap_verdict_pressure: Swap is climbing ({{swap}}) while available memory falls ({{available}}). Those two together are real pressure rather than leftover cold pages — the machine is paying for memory with disk. This is the one worth acting on.
host.swap_verdict_filling: Swap is growing ({{swap}}), but available memory is holding steady. That is the kernel moving cold pages out of the way, not the machine running short.
host.swap_verdict_cold: Old or cold pages left over from an earlier squeeze. Linux does not pull pages back out of swap just because RAM frees up, so this figure stays where it is until something touches them — a high-water mark, not a measure of now. No current shortage: watch for swap rising while available memory falls, which is a different thing entirely.
host.swap_verdict_waiting: Not enough readings yet to say whether this is left over or still growing — that needs about half an hour of history.
host.services_no_history: No service history yet — this needs a few readings to build up.
host.services_chart_empty: Not enough service history to draw yet
host.services_counter_rate_help: Counters differentiated into a rate; a gap means the service restarted.
host.io_collector_missing: The host collector is not installed.
host.io_needs_two_readings: Needs two host readings before a rate can be worked out.
host.io_no_counters: No device counters recorded for this range.
host.io_busiest_moment: Busiest moment: {{rate}} at {{at}} — the busiest device was {{saturation}}% saturated.
host.io_counter_restarts: {{readings, number}} readings could not be turned into a rate, because the counters restarted — that is a reboot.
host.walk_pending: A walk was requested {{ago}} and is waiting for the next host collection. It runs on the collector's schedule — every five minutes with the suggested crontab line.
host.walk_requested: Requested. The host collector will walk the disk on its next run.
host.one_reading: Only one host reading so far
host.add_root_collector_cron: As root — SSH in or use WHM's Terminal — add this to root's crontab with crontab -e:
host.run_collector_once: Then run it once by hand to see what it finds: {{command}}
auth.recovery_codes_title: Create new one-time recovery codes after confirming your authenticator
uptime.restart_explanation: Boot time moved, so the machine did restart. It came back at {{booted}}; it went down at some point after the last reading, so this is an upper bound rather than a measurement.
uptime.gap_collector_not_running: Boot time was unchanged either side, so the machine ran straight through this — it was up, and the collector was not running.
uptime.gap_before_tracking: These readings predate boot-time recording, so whether the machine restarted here cannot be told. Not an outage — just a stretch that cannot be classified. Gaps from now on will say which.
uptime.gap_unknown: No boot time either side to compare, so whether the machine stayed up through this cannot be told from these readings.

health.no_inline_styles_help: index.html carries a style="" attribute, which the content security policy blocks — the rule silently does not apply. Move it into index.css.

ai.chat_add_help: It is working. This goes in now and it reads it on its next turn.
system.snapshot_empty: No copies have been made. One is written when a note asks for it — a consistent copy of both databases, for looking at after the readings it is about have been rolled up.
system.snapshot_delete_confirm:
Delete {{name}}?

It is {{size}} and nothing else has a copy.
database.host_unreadable: Present but not readable by this account, or not there at all.
database.indexes_note: Indexes are counted against the table they belong to. On a busy table an index can be close to half the total, and listing them separately makes every table look cheaper than it is.
storage.account_help: A monitor that fills the disk it is watching has failed in the most embarrassing way available to it. This is what this account’s database holds, what each part of it costs, and — the part that is usually missing — what the file will settle at if nobody touches the settings again. A table set to keep 400 days that has been collecting for thirty is at under a tenth of its eventual size, and nothing else here says so.
storage.host_help: Written by root’s collector, and read-only from here. This account can usually open it to read and should never be the thing that rewrites it — a rewrite started from here would leave a file the collector could no longer write. Where it cannot be opened at all, that is said rather than shown as zeros.
auth.sign_in_help: Reveals real paths and enables deleting.
